title: Present in every land
hook: the Jaap salutes the One who dwells in every country and every garb

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhai, without fear, and your line, fearless like him. Did you do one thing you'd been putting off? Today, Jaap looks out across the whole map. Day three hundred fifty-three.

Open a map of gurdwaras on your phone and zoom out. Southall, in west London. Surrey, near Vancouver. Yuba City in California. Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur, Melbourne, Singapore, a small town in northern Italy. Little markers scattered across the map. Behind each one, someone who left Punjab, carried the Guru's words in a suitcase, and found that the morning prayers still worked in a new time zone. Long before any of that, the Tenth Guru wrote praise that fits every one of those places. Today: present in every land.
screen: `A MAP OF GURDWARAS, ZOOMED OUT.` → `MARKERS SCATTERED ACROSS THE MAP.` → `THE PRAYERS WORK IN A NEW TIME ZONE.`

segments.voice: Throughout Jaap, the One is saluted as dwelling everywhere: in every country, in every kind of dress, in water and on land. One short chachari line says it in four words: jale hain, thale hain. You are in the water. You are on the land. And near its very end, Jaap calls the One chatar chakkar vartee, present in all four directions, every point of the compass. Think about what every garb means in the Guru's world. Clothing told everyone who you were: a Hindu holy man's saffron, a Muslim scholar's robe, a soldier's armor, a farmer's rough cotton, a queen's silk. Jaap salutes the One in all of them, and Sikhs read it plainly: no land is holier by birth, and no costume is closer to the Divine. Sikhs have a long habit of living that line. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak walking for years, east toward Assam, south toward Sri Lanka, north into the mountains, west as far as Mecca and Baghdad, sitting with people of every faith he met. And today Sikhs pray the Ardas in Toronto and Birmingham and Bangkok with the same closing words you met at the end of year one: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Punjab. The good of all. In that reading, every land is somewhere to pray, and every stranger in every garb is someone the One is already with.
screen: `EVERY COUNTRY, EVERY GARB.` · `JALE HAIN, THALE HAIN: WATER AND LAND.` · `CHATAR CHAKKAR VARTEE: ALL DIRECTIONS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `IN EVERY LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a faraway place kindly. Choose somewhere you've never been, or somewhere in the news, or the place your family came from. Picture it as clearly as you can: the streets, the weather, the people waking up or going to sleep there right now. Breathe in, and picture them. Breathe out, and wish them well, plainly: may they be safe, may they be fed. If you pray, you can hold them in the words sarbat da bhala. The bell holds the time.
Des. A country or land — Jaap salutes the One in every des and every garb, in water and on land, in all four directions.
Your line: in every land. Today, when you hear a place name in the news, any place at all, wish the people there well for one breath. Day three hundred fifty-three.

screen: `DAY 353 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BEYOND THE FEAR OF DEATH.`

howItsDone: Sikhs around the world recite Jaap Sahib in the same words every morning, and gurdwaras far from Punjab close their gatherings with the Ardas's prayer for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

fork.setup: you're a Sikh who has moved from Punjab to a new country with your gutka in your suitcase. does Jaap's praise still fit?
options: no: the prayers belong to Punjab.
yes: Jaap salutes the One in every land and every garb.
only in a gurdwara built like the ones at home.
fork.reveal: jale hain, thale hain: in water and on land, in every country. the morning prayers work in every time zone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: des, a country or land; Jaap salutes the One in every des and every bhes, garb.

trapdoor: what you thought: present in every land means God is everywhere, vaguely.
what it means: no land or costume is closer to the One; every place is somewhere to pray, every stranger someone the One is with.
what a scholar hears: Jaap's des/bhes pairing and jale hain, thale hain express sarab viapak (all-pervading); chatar chakkar vartee recurs in the final stanza.

notes: The exact Jaap line for 'every country and every garb' (e.g., 'namo sarab dese, namo sarab bhese') is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm stanza and wording.
'jale hain, thale hain' as a chachari line: confirm.
'chatar chakkar vartee' placed in the final stanza (199); confirm. Day 356 also covers the closing stanzas.
